title: Lease-based regional steering with progressive fallback matrix and tenant QoS budgets
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Problem: During capacity pressure events we currently make binary routing decisions that either keep traffic on dedicated lanes or send everything to hosted endpoints. This causes latency spikes for some tenants and unexpected cost increases for others. We need a graceful, lease-based steering mechanism that enforces per-tenant QoS budgets and a progressive fallback matrix of model variants and tiers so that applications degrade predictably instead of failing hard.

Goals: implement a lease-backed regional steering layer that: (1) holds soft reservations for active tenants (short-lived leases that indicate preferred region/tier), (2) supports progressive fallback rules to select alternative model variants by cost/latency/quality trade-offs, (3) enforces tenant QoS budgets (burst credits + steady-state budget) to avoid noisy neighbors, and (4) exposes observability and runbooks for operators.

Non-goals: this ticket does not change admission control for initial connection setup, nor does it modify on-prem networking. It builds on existing capacity accounting and hosted fallback primitives.

Proposed approach:
- Lease broker: lightweight in-memory lease service with persistence to Redis for quick recovery. Leases are short (10–60s) and include: tenant_id, preferred_region, preferred_tier, token_bucket_state, and a lease_version.
- Steering decision flow: evaluation order = (1) lease check + tenant budget, (2) capacity-aware verification of preferred lane, (3) progressive fallback matrix evaluation to pick model variant (quantized / lower-context / batched) and tier (dedicated->reserved-low->hosted-surface), (4) side-channel notify for async pre-warm of KV cache.
- Progressive fallback matrix: a configurable table ordered by expected latency and cost with acceptance thresholds expressed as target_p90_latency and quality_loss_pct. Matrix entries are annotated with rollback weight for A/B experiments.
- Tenant QoS budgets: per-tenant token bucket persisted to Redis with refill rules and a small burst cap. If tenant budget exhausted, apply permissive demotion policy (sampled degraded responses + throttled tokens) rather than full rejection.
- Safeguards / circuit breakers: multi-dimensional triggers (regional errors, latency, error-rate, capacity fill) that can: pause new leases, widen fallback tolerances, or route to transparent slowdown mode. All triggers timestamped and auditable.

Trade-offs considered:
- Lease duration shorter -> more responsive but more churn and master load. Chosen compromise is 20s default with backoff for hot tenants.
- Local consistency vs speed: strong cross-region consistency costs latency; we use optimistic leases with conflict detection and periodic reconciliation to keep decisions fast.
- Quality vs cost: fallbacks include lower-precision variants; we attach quality_loss_pct thresholds so PMs can tune acceptability per route.

Risks: Redis becoming a bottleneck (mitigated with sharded keys + local caches), complexity in rollout causing surprise degradations (mitigated via canary sampling and automatic rollback rules).
acceptance_criteria: Lease broker deployed behind feature flag with functional tests: create/renew/revoke leases
Routing decision path can read lease + token bucket and select fallback variant according to matrix
Per-tenant burst token bucket enforced for at least 1000 tenants in staging without >1% additional p95 latency
Progressive fallback matrix in config service and editable by PM/ops with change audit
Dashboard showing lease metrics, fallback activations, tenant budget violations, and rollback triggers
Runbook for operators including steps to pause leases, widen fallbacks, and rollback to previous routing logic
plan: Week 1: Design doc + API spec (lease schema, token bucket), run design review (Confluence link in attachments)
Week 2: Implement lease broker prototype + unit tests; local Redis-backed persistence; add metrics hooks
Week 3: Integrate steering flow into router; implement progressive fallback matrix config; e2e tests against simulated capacity
Week 4: Staging canary with 5% traffic for a set of low-risk tenants; monitor dashboards and adjust thresholds
Week 5: Expand canary to medium-risk tenants, perform load test at scale; finalize runbook; prepare release notes
